# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a potentially life-threatening form of heart failure that develops toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery in women without another identifiable cause of cardiac dysfunction. The first systematic case definition emerged from a 2000 National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) and Office of Rare Diseases workshop, which characterised PPCM as a rare life-threatening cardiomyopathy of unknown cause that occurs in the peripartum period in previously healthy women, convened to foster a systematic review of information and develop recommendations for research and education [1]. In 2010, the Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) refined this, defining PPCM as an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure secondary to left ventricular systolic dysfunction toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, a diagnosis of exclusion in which the left ventricle may not be dilated but the ejection fraction is nearly always reduced below 45% [2]. A 2019 HFA position statement reaffirmed these criteria and emphasised that because shortness of breath, fatigue, and leg oedema are common in the peripartum period, a high index of suspicion is required, and natriuretic peptides, electrocardiography, and echocardiography are recommended to promptly diagnose or exclude heart failure [3].

## Epidemiology

Incidence varies markedly by geography and ethnicity. The incidence was highest, around 1 in 102 deliveries, in Nigeria and lowest, approximately 1 in 15,533 births, in Japan [4]. In the United States, a population-based study reported an incidence of 4.84 per 10,000 live births among 227,224 eligible women [5], with independent predictors including maternal age of 25 years or older, African American and Filipino ethnicity, high parity, multiple gestation, severe anemia, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy [5]. A nationwide analysis showed that from 2004 to 2011 the incidence of PPCM increased in the United States, while cardiogenic shock, use of mechanical circulatory support, and in-hospital mortality all increased [6]. Disparities in outcome are striking: in the IPAC cohort, Black women presented with more severe cardiomyopathy and had less recovery of cardiac function than White women on follow-up [7].

## Pathophysiology

A major conceptual advance came in 2007, when investigators demonstrated that female mice with a cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Stat3 develop PPCM, with enhanced cardiac cathepsin D activity associated with generation of a cleaved antiangiogenic and proapoptotic 16-kDa form of the nursing hormone prolactin [8]. Downstream signalling was subsequently clarified: 16-kDa prolactin induces microRNA-146a expression in endothelial cells, attenuating angiogenesis through downregulation of NRAS, and is transported via exosomes to cardiomyocytes where it impairs metabolism [9]. A complementary "two-hit" vascular hypothesis arose from work showing that PPCM occurs more frequently in pre-eclampsia and multiple gestation; mice lacking cardiac PGC-1α develop profound PPCM that is rescued by pro-angiogenic therapy, and the placenta in late gestation secretes VEGF inhibitors such as soluble FLT1 [10]. These models converge on the notion that PPCM is in large part a vascular disease triggered by the hormonal milieu of the peripartum period [11].

A genetic contribution is now well established. In 172 women with PPCM, 26 distinct rare truncating variants were identified in eight genes, with a prevalence of truncating variants (15%) significantly higher than in a reference population (4.7%) but similar to that in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy (17%) [12]. Two-thirds of these variants were in TTN, and their presence correlated with a lower ejection fraction at one-year follow-up [12]. Consistent with this, the ESC notes that around 15–20% of patients with peripartum heart failure carry mutations in genes such as titin, beta-myosin heavy chain, MYBPC3, lamin A/C, or SCN5A [3].

## Diagnosis and clinical presentation

PPCM remains a diagnosis of exclusion. Important differential diagnoses include pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, hypertensive heart disease during pregnancy, and pre-existing heart disease, and since no specific confirmatory test exists, these must be considered [3]. Heart failure symptoms mimic those of normal pregnancy, often delaying diagnosis, so echocardiography demonstrating decreased myocardial function is essential [13].

## Management and disease-specific therapy

Standard care follows guideline-directed therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, adjusted for pregnancy and lactation. The prolactin hypothesis prompted trials of bromocriptine. In a multicentre randomized study, 63 PPCM patients with LVEF ≤35% received short- or long-term bromocriptine added to standard heart failure therapy, and inhibition of prolactin release was associated with a high recovery rate and a very low rate of adverse outcome [14]. However, a critical unanswered question is whether bromocriptine adds to the effectiveness of guideline therapy, as the study had no non-use control group [15], and a systematic review found that data on the efficacy of bromocriptine on LV function and mortality are mixed and limited to small, underpowered studies [16].

## Outcomes and subsequent pregnancy

Prognosis is variable. In the North American IPAC study, which enrolled and followed 100 women with PPCM through one year postpartum [17], event-free survival at one year was 93%, transplant-free survival was 95%, and at 12 months 72% of patients achieved an LVEF ≥50% [17]. The global ESC EORP registry, which included participants from 49 countries [18], found that just under half of deaths occurred within 30 days of diagnosis, just under half of women experienced myocardial recovery within six months, and neonatal death occurred in 5% [18]. A landmark study of subsequent pregnancies showed that subsequent pregnancy is associated with a significant decrease in left ventricular function and can result in clinical deterioration and even death [19], an observation reinforced by the IPAC investigators' finding that the pre-pregnancy LVEF is the strongest predictor of outcomes in a subsequent pregnancy [20].

## Conclusion

PPCM is an uncommon but serious pregnancy-associated heart failure whose understanding has advanced from a disorder of "unknown cause" to one driven by hormonally triggered vascular injury acting on a genetically susceptible myocardium. Early recognition, guideline-directed heart failure therapy, multidisciplinary cardio-obstetric care, and careful counselling regarding future pregnancies remain the cornerstones of management while disease-specific therapies continue to be evaluated.
